extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_short: assessing prior art and defenses in patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on statutory and case-law standards for pleading, proving, and evaluating defenses to patent infringement based on prior publication, prior use, authorship, and disclaimers. Focuses on notice requirements, what counts as a defeating publication or prior specification, and the legal effect of disclaimers and related statutory provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory special matters (1870 §61) — defenses defendant may plead
rubrics_metrics.description: In any action for infringement the defendant may plead the general issue and, having given notice thirty days before trial, may prove any one or more of the following special matters: (First) the patentee's specification was made to contain less than the whole truth or more than is necessary; (Second) the patentee surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent for that which was in fact invented by another who was using reasonable diligence; (Third) it had been patented or described in some printed publication prior to the supposed invention; (Fourth) he was not the original and first inventor or discoverer of any material and substantial part of the thing patented; (Fifth) it had been in public use or on sale in this country for more than two years before his application or had been abandoned to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one or more of these special matters alleged are found for the defendant, judgment shall be rendered for him with costs. The statute allows like defenses in equity suits, with like notice and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory notice period (30 days) for asserting special matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant must give notice in writing to the plaintiff or his attorney thirty days before trial in order to prove the special matters enumerated by statute (1870 §61).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 30‑day written notice is a statutory precondition to offering proof of these defenses at trial; the notice must be sufficiently particular (see related notice specificity criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice content specificity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice must be 'so full and particular as reasonably to answer the end in view' — it should relieve the patentee from useless inquiries and enable him to fix with precision upon what is relied on and prepare to meet it at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant should identify particulars he knows and can safely state (e.g., pages or titles in publications, names and residences of prior inventors, dates of patents, where and by whom prior use occurred). Vague notices (e.g., pointing to a 1,300 page volume without page or article references) are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to specify place in prior publication or place of prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: When alleging that an invention was described in a public work or that a person had prior use/knowledge, the defendant must specify the book and the place (e.g., page, article) where the description is to be found and where the prior use occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to state the place in the work or where a named person's prior use occurred renders the book or evidence incompetent under the statute; the notice must enable the patentee to identify and investigate the asserted prior matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'public work' vs 'printed publication' — accessibility to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Although statutes use both 'some public work' and 'any printed publication', the intended construction is that the description must have been printed and published so as to be accessible to the public where published; private, obscure, or singular circulations that are not publicly accessible should not be treated as defeating publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a given printing/issue made the matter accessible to the public is a question of fact (for the jury) under the surrounding circumstances; courts distinguish between general circulation works and isolated obscure copies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication in law occurs when a work is offered for sale (no sale necessary)
rubrics_metrics.description: A foreign book sent to a bookseller and exposed in the publisher's/bookseller's shop for the purpose of sale constitutes a publication in law in the jurisdiction — it is not necessary to prove actual sale of copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat the moment the book is offered for sale publicly as sufficient to make the invention part of the public stock of information (illustrated in Lang v. Gisborne).

rubrics_metrics.name: What qualifies as a 'description' that defeats novelty — must enable practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior description must of itself enable the public, without further invention, to practise the invention; it must approach the character of a specification by serving as a direction for making, doing, or practising the thing which is the subject of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere speculation, experimental hints, or suggestions that do not give practical directions will not defeat a patent. The description must give the means of knowledge sufficient for the public to practise the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seymour v. Osborne test for foreign publications
rubrics_metrics.description: "Patented inventions cannot be superseded by the mere introduction of a foreign publication of the kind, though of prior date, unless the description and drawings contain and exhibit a substantial representation of the patented improvement, in such full, clear, and exact terms as to enable any person, skilled in the art or science ... to make, construct, and practise the invention to the same practical extent ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague or general representations in a publication will not support a defense; the prior publication must be a complete and operative account capable of being put into practical operation by a skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of foreign prior knowledge/use
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere previous knowledge or use of the thing in a foreign country will not defeat a patent granted here to an original inventor, provided the thing had not been previously patented or described in a printed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 62 (statute of 1870) preserves patents against defeat by mere foreign use or knowledge unless the foreign matter was in a patent or printed publication accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers (Act of March 3, 1837 §§7 & 9) — when and how they operate
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patentee, through inadvertence, accident, or mistake, has claimed more than he was the original inventor of, and some material and substantial part truly and justly belongs to him, he (or his successors) may make a written disclaimer of such parts, stating the extent of his interest; the disclaimer must be attested by witnesses, recorded in the Patent Office on payment of ten dollars, and will be considered part of the original specification to the extent of the disclaimant's interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer filed before suit may permit the plaintiff to recover costs on proving infringement of the undisclaimed part; a disclaimer filed during a suit will not afford benefit in that suit (per Reed v. Cutter). Unreasonable neglect or delay in filing a disclaimer may prevent its benefits and constitute a defense to suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial validity where specification embraces more than inventor's contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a specification embraces more than that of which the patentee was the first inventor, the patent shall be deemed good and valid for so much of the invention as shall be truly and bona fide his own, provided it is a material and substantial part and definitely distinguishable from other parts claimed without right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patentee may maintain suit for infringement of the bona fide part, but will not be entitled to recover costs unless he had entered a disclaimer at the Patent Office prior to commencing suit; unreasonable delay in entering the disclaimer may bar its benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of prior patent specifications — mere hints insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defense is a prior patent specification, it is not sufficient that the earlier specification contain a mere hint of the process or invention claimed in the subsequent patent; the prior specification must contain more than a hint — a substantial representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English authorities and the House of Lords hold that incomplete prior specifications that only suggest an invention do not defeat a later patent for that invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences when a special matter is proved
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one or more of the special matters set out in the statute are proved for the defendant, judgment shall be rendered for him with costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consequence applies in actions at law and, by analogous procedure and notice, in suits in equity.
